articles.title: A-Level results day: Rochdale students discover what comes next
articles.excerpt: Students across Rochdale are receiving their A-Level results today, as the town's sixth form record comes under the spotlight and Rochdale MP Paul Waugh begins his new role at the Department for Education.
articles.content_html:
Students across Rochdale have been opening their A-Level results today, bringing two years of study, examinations and anxious waiting to an end as young people discover whether they have secured university places, apprenticeships or their next step into employment.

Results day on Thursday 13 August comes during another strong year nationally. Across the UK, 28.5% of A-Level entries were awarded an A* or A, while in England the figure was 28.3%. More than 262,000 UK 18-year-olds had been accepted onto university courses by results day.

In the North West, 26.5% of A-Level entries received an A* or A in 2026, compared with 26.6% in 2025 and 23.5% in 2019. The figures continue to show a substantial regional divide, with London recording 32.7% of entries at A* or A this year.

For Rochdale, particular attention falls on Rochdale Sixth Form College, which has developed a strong academic record since opening in September 2010. The college was created following longstanding concerns about post-16 attainment in the borough and the number of local students travelling outside Rochdale for sixth-form education.

The college's early results quickly attracted national attention. It was ranked second among sixth form colleges for value added in Department for Education performance tables in 2013 and later achieved first place for A-Level progress for several consecutive years. By January 2019 it had been ranked first in Department for Education performance tables for five years running, and in 2021 it won Sixth Form College of the Year at the Tes FE Awards.

More recent government performance data has continued to show strong progress. Department for Education figures for 2024 recorded an average A-Level result of B- at Rochdale Sixth Form College and an A-Level progress score of +0.41, classified as well above average. The 2025 figures again recorded an average result of B-, with an average point score of 37.33 and a progress measure of +0.48, also classified as well above average.

The historical picture matters because Rochdale Sixth Form College was established in part to tackle a period in which the borough's A-Level performance had lagged behind national averages. Its subsequent performance provides a significant contrast with the concerns that led to the college being established more than 15 years ago.

Today's results are also notable politically because Rochdale's MP, Paul Waugh, has recently joined the Department for Education. Mr Waugh was appointed Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Education in July 2026, giving Rochdale a direct connection to national education policy.

Today's A-Level cohort completed almost all of its education before Mr Waugh entered the department, so the 2026 results cannot reasonably be attributed to his tenure. Future results, however, will increasingly provide part of the national record against which the Government's education policies — and the ministers responsible for them — are judged.

That will be particularly relevant in areas such as Rochdale because regional inequality remains one of the clearest challenges facing education ministers. This year's figures show 32.7% of A-Level entries in London receiving A* or A, compared with 26.5% in the North West and 23.1% in both the North East and East Midlands.

For students receiving their results today, however, national statistics and ministerial records are unlikely to be the immediate priority. For some, the results will confirm university places they have worked towards for years. Others will move into apprenticeships, employment or further study, while students who have missed required grades can consider Clearing and alternative routes.

Whatever the individual results, today marks the end of one chapter for Rochdale's students and the beginning of another.

articles.title: Burnley Man Banned from Keeping Animals After Dog Found Emaciated in Rochdale Home
articles.excerpt: A man has received a 15-year ban on keeping animals after an emaciated dog was discovered in a Rochdale property. Paul Lewis Dawson was sentenced at Tameside Magistrates' Court for animal welfare offences.
articles.content_html:
A man has been banned from keeping animals for 15 years after an emaciated dog was found living in unsanitary conditions at a property in Rochdale. Paul Lewis Dawson, 37, of Brownside Road in Burnley, pleaded guilty to three offences under the Animal Welfare Act 2006 at Tameside Magistrates' Court on 31 July.

The RSPCA began investigating on 6 August 2025 after receiving reports about a bullbreed dog named Kano being left unattended at a property on Alice Street in Rochdale. RSPCA inspector Beth Fazackerley and animal rescue officer Francesca Iraci attended the address, where they observed Kano through the keyhole and noted he appeared very skinny. After no one answered the door, they pushed wet dog food through the letterbox, which Kano ate.

Later that evening, the RSPCA returned with a police officer after obtaining a warrant. Upon entering the property, Kano was found to be in poor condition, having difficulty standing and displaying visible signs of distress. The dog was covered in fleas, had wounds on his body, and was suffering from severe weight loss and anaemia due to an insufficient diet. Rubbish and faeces were found throughout the property, creating an unsuitable living environment for the animal.

Dawson received a 22-week prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, and was ordered to complete 18 Rehabilitation Activity Requirement days and 80 hours of unpaid work, in addition to paying £400 in costs. The judge described the case as "the most serious case of animal cruelty I have ever dealt with." Kano has since been taken into the care of the RSPCA and has recovered.

The circulating footage is nevertheless likely to prompt questions about whether further investigation or inspection is required. Food businesses are required to follow hygiene controls designed to protect food from contamination during storage, preparation and handling.

Residents concerned about food hygiene at a premises can report their concerns to the relevant local authority environmental-health service.

She has also placed housing, economic growth and reducing inequalities among the central issues facing Greater Manchester.

Those priorities are particularly relevant to Rochdale, where transport connectivity, town-centre investment, housing and access to opportunity remain major local issues.

Before becoming mayor, Craig led Manchester City Council from December 2021 and held Greater Manchester responsibilities for economy, business and inclusive growth. She was awarded an OBE in March 2026 for services to local government.

Her election followed the departure of Andy Burnham from the mayoralty. Craig won the contest after the count proceeded to a second round, defeating Reform UK's Sian Astley.

Today's Rochdale visit will therefore be watched for signs of how the new mayor intends to translate her city-region promises into action for individual boroughs outside Manchester city centre.

articles.title: LIVE: GMP student officer arrested on suspicion of rape and kidnap after M62 pursuit
articles.excerpt: LIVE updates after a 23-year-old Greater Manchester Police student officer was arrested on suspicion of rape, kidnap and dangerous driving following a pursuit on the M62.
articles.content_html:
LIVE UPDATES — This story is being updated as further confirmed information becomes available.

18:50 — Greater Manchester Police says it is committed to working with the Crown Prosecution Service to bring the case to court as quickly as possible, while also accelerating misconduct proceedings within police regulations. Assistant Chief Constable Mark Dexter said the allegations were deeply concerning and disturbing and said all necessary and decisive action would be taken in the interests of the woman and the public.

GMP has confirmed its Professional Standards Directorate carried out an initial review of the officer's vetting and found it had been completed without any reason for concern. The force stressed that this did not lessen the severity of the allegations.

articles.title: This week in Rochdale, 100 years ago: the town captured from the air in August 1926
articles.excerpt: Exactly a century ago this month, aerial photographers captured remarkable views of Rochdale's Town Hall, Yorkshire Street, railway station, Broadfield Park and industrial works — preserving the town as it looked in August 1926.
articles.content_html:
One hundred years ago this week, Rochdale was a very different town — but thanks to a remarkable series of aerial photographs taken in August 1926, we can still see it almost street by street.

The images, held by the Britain From Above archive, show a dense industrial town of mills, railway infrastructure, tramways, terraced streets and civic buildings. They provide one of the clearest surviving visual records of Rochdale in the inter-war period.

Yorkshire Street was photographed from the air in August 1926 under reference EPW016788. The view shows the familiar line of the street threading through tightly packed buildings, with factories, chimneys and terraced housing occupying much of the surrounding landscape. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016788

Rochdale railway station was also captured that month under reference EPW016784. The photograph shows not only the station but the extraordinary concentration of railway sidings, engineering works and industrial premises that once surrounded this part of the town. The archive identifies features including railway works, cotton mills, a goods shed and the Rochdale Canal terminal basin. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016784

Another image, EPW016791, looks across Town Hall Square. It records landmarks that remain instantly recognisable alongside features which have since vanished or changed beyond recognition. Archive annotations identify St Chad's, the Esplanade, Rochdale Post Office, Drake Street, tramcars and the Rochdale War Memorial while it was still under construction. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016791

Broadfield Park was photographed in the same month under reference EPW016782, giving another extraordinary perspective across the civic heart of Rochdale. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016782

The industrial scale of the town is perhaps most obvious in the August 1926 photographs of Fishwick Street. Image EPW016789 records the railway works there, reflecting the huge engineering and manufacturing presence which once surrounded Rochdale's rail network. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016789

Even before that August series, an Aerofilms photograph taken on 6 August 1926 captured Rochdale Road crossing the railway and Rochdale Canal at Slattocks. The image, EPW016440, preserves a landscape where canal, railway and road infrastructure sat side by side — the transport arteries which helped power the borough's industrial economy. View the original image: https://www.britainfromabove.org.uk/en/image/EPW016440

What is striking about these photographs is not simply what has disappeared. It is how much remains legible. The Town Hall, St Chad's, major road alignments and parts of the railway landscape allow modern residents to orient themselves inside a town photographed from an aircraft a century ago.

The photographs also capture Rochdale during a period of profound change. The borough remained heavily industrial, public transport still included corporation tramcars, and mills and engineering works dominated huge areas which today contain housing, roads, offices and redeveloped land.

The Rochdale Observer itself was already a long-established part of town life by 1926, having first appeared in 1856. Its surviving archive means future editions of Rochdale Daily's '100 Years Ago' feature can go beyond photographs and recover the stories residents were actually reading — crime reports, council debates, sport, advertisements, court cases, births, deaths and the everyday incidents which made up life in the borough.

For this first edition, though, the photographs tell their own story. They allow us to look down on Rochdale exactly a century ago and recognise both the town we inherited and the one that disappeared.

Rochdale Daily intends to make 'This Week in Rochdale — 100 Years Ago' a recurring history feature throughout the centenary year.

articles.title: Are our reservoirs recovering after Rochdale's exceptionally dry summer?
articles.excerpt: North West reservoir stocks fell sharply during July, but the latest verified figures show the region entered the dry spell with considerably more water in storage than at the same point last year.
articles.content_html:
After weeks of heat, dry ground and remarkably little rainfall, attention is turning to the North West's reservoirs — and whether the return of more changeable weather has begun to undo the damage.

The short answer is: not yet, based on the latest reservoir figures Rochdale Daily has been able to verify — although the overall regional position remains considerably better than it was this time last year.

United Utilities publishes figures covering the major reservoir systems supplying the North West. For the week ending 19 July, total regional reservoir storage stood at 70.6%. That was down 4.1 percentage points in just one week and slightly below the 72.7% average for that point in the year.

Of particular interest to Rochdale are United Utilities' Pennine sources. These were at 64.3% capacity by 19 July, having fallen four percentage points in a week. The normal level for that point in the year is 66.6%.

There is some reassuring context. At the same point last year, the Pennine sources were at just 42.2%. That means that despite this summer's prolonged dry weather, Pennine storage remained more than 20 percentage points higher than during the equivalent week of 2025.

Haweswater and Thirlmere — enormously important components of the North West's water-supply system — stood at a combined 67%. That represented a fall of 4.7 percentage points in a week, although it remained above the 64% seasonal average and above last year's 60.3%. At Thirlmere itself, the water surface was recorded at 4.01 metres below top water level.

Across the major reservoir groups, regional storage was 70.6%, Pennine sources 64.3%, Haweswater and Thirlmere 67%, Dee and Vyrnwy 76.5%, and Carlisle 66.8%. Every major group recorded a weekly decline, with Carlisle falling nine percentage points in a week.

So will a few rainy days refill them? Unfortunately, reservoirs do not work quite that quickly. Rain falling onto Rochdale does not translate immediately into an equivalent rise in reservoir storage. After a prolonged dry spell, rainfall must interact with dry soils, vegetation, rivers and the wider catchment before significant quantities reach reservoirs, while homes and businesses continue using water every day.

This is why several genuinely wet periods — rather than a couple of showers — can be required before reservoir levels show a meaningful and sustained recovery. The North West also operates as an interconnected water-supply system, meaning Rochdale's water security cannot be judged simply by looking at the nearest reservoir and seeing how full it appears.

The dry conditions have accompanied an exceptionally hot start to summer. By the middle of July, England and Wales had each received only around 34% of their normal rainfall for the entire summer season, despite being halfway through meteorological summer. Some locations had recorded no measurable July rainfall at all by that point.

Temperatures have also been extraordinary. By 15 July, the UK had already experienced more days above 30C during 2026 than occurred during the whole of the famously hot summer of 1976.

The Environment Agency has consequently been closely monitoring water resources across England, while United Utilities was under enhanced monitoring and operations for its Haweswater and Carlisle water-resource zones during July. Wildfires across Greater Manchester, Cheshire and Derbyshire created additional pressure, with significant quantities of water also required for firefighting.

The figures require perspective. Storage has fallen substantially and the Pennine system was below its seasonal average in the latest verified snapshot, but this is not the same situation as last summer. Pennine sources being at 64.3% compared with 42.2% at the same point in 2025 gives the region considerably more resilience. Haweswater and Thirlmere were also above both their seasonal average and last year's level.

The key question now is what happens during August. Several weeks of regular rainfall could begin rebuilding water resources. A return to prolonged heat and dry weather, however, would place further pressure on reservoir stocks at precisely the time when summer water demand remains high.

For Rochdale residents looking at exposed reservoir banks and wondering whether recent rain means the problem is over, the answer is more complicated: the North West entered the dry spell with a healthier reserve than last year, but reservoir stocks have been falling quickly and recovery requires sustained rainfall rather than the occasional wet day.

Rochdale Daily will continue tracking reservoir levels as new figures are published.

articles.title: Inside abandoned Simpson Clough Paper Mill — and why urban exploration carries serious risks
articles.excerpt: A YouTube video has taken viewers inside the abandoned Simpson Clough Paper Mill near Rochdale, revealing remnants of its industrial past while highlighting the fascination — and dangers — of urban exploration.
articles.content_html:
An abandoned paper mill near Rochdale where machinery, equipment and remnants of its working life appear to have been left behind has been documented by urban explorers.

Footage titled 'We Found The ABANDONED Simpson Clough Paper Mill Hidden In Rochdale With Everything Left Behind!' takes viewers inside Simpson Clough Mill, offering a glimpse into an industrial site normally hidden from public view.

Watch the exploration: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pCnxD574cB8

The mill has a long industrial history. Local historical records describe Simpson Clough Mills as beginning as a fulling mill in the 1840s before being purchased by Cromptons in 1939, used for food storage during the Second World War and converted to paper manufacture after the war. The site later operated as Union Papertech and closed in January 2023.

The footage captures much of what has made so-called urban exploration, or urbex, enormously popular online. Instead of seeing industrial history restored and labelled inside a museum, viewers see workplaces in their abandoned state: machinery, offices, workshops and the gradual effects of time and nature.

For a borough whose identity was profoundly shaped by mills, manufacturing and the Industrial Revolution, sites such as Simpson Clough have an obvious historical fascination. They can provide a visual record of workplaces where generations of people spent their working lives.

But urban exploration has another side which should not be overlooked. Abandoned industrial buildings can be extremely dangerous. Water penetration, corrosion, structural deterioration and years without routine maintenance can leave floors, roofs and staircases unsafe. Broken glass, exposed metal, electrical hazards, contaminated water and hazardous materials can create further risks.

Someone injured deep inside a large former industrial complex may also be difficult for emergency services to locate and rescue.

The legal position is more complicated than saying that entering every abandoned building automatically amounts to a criminal offence. Ordinary trespass in England and Wales is generally a civil matter, but abandoned buildings and the land surrounding them still have owners. Entering private property without permission can amount to trespass, while damaging fences, doors or windows, taking property, or entering certain protected sites can raise separate criminal issues.

Rochdale Daily does not know whether the people responsible for the Simpson Clough footage had permission to enter the site and makes no allegation that any offence was committed.

The fascination with urbex is nevertheless understandable. There is something extraordinary about seeing a workplace after the workers have gone. Desks, machinery and ordinary objects can become accidental historical artefacts, and videos produced by explorers have created an informal online record of parts of Britain's disappearing industrial landscape.

The challenge is preserving that history without people putting themselves in danger or entering places unlawfully. Property owners can grant controlled access to photographers, historians and filmmakers, while heritage organisations can document industrial buildings before redevelopment or demolition.

That could be particularly valuable around Rochdale, Heywood and the surrounding valleys, where surviving industrial sites tell an important part of the borough's story.

Simpson Clough is another reminder that extraordinary pieces of local industrial history can sit quietly behind walls and fences long after their original purpose has disappeared. They are fascinating to see — but no photograph or video is worth serious injury to obtain.

Rochdale Daily does not encourage entry onto private, abandoned or restricted property without permission. Anyone wishing to document a disused site should seek the landowner's permission and follow appropriate safety requirements.

articles.title: Comment: Rochdale Canal should be the jewel in the town's crown
articles.excerpt: Steven Parker of the Rochdale Canal Group argues that a living canal basin filled with boats, heritage, independent businesses and public space could bring visitors, jobs and regeneration to Rochdale.
articles.content_html:
This is a comment article by Steven Parker of the Rochdale Canal Group. The views expressed are his own.

Rochdale Branch Canal

Industrial units will not bring visitors to Rochdale, but a living canal basin filled with boats, a heritage centre, café, independent shops and exhibition space most definitely will.

Our historic canals should be the jewel in Rochdale's crown, but instead they languish neglected and forgotten.

The time is right for real change along the Rochdale Canal corridor, and we must be instrumental in making it happen.

A revitalised canal corridor has the potential to offer far more than an attractive waterside environment. Done properly, regeneration could create environmental improvements, attract visitors, support independent businesses, create employment and reconnect Rochdale with an extraordinary part of its industrial heritage.

A living canal basin would give people a reason to spend time in Rochdale rather than simply pass through it. Boats bring movement and activity. A heritage centre could tell the story of the canal and the industries it once served. Cafés, independent shops and exhibition spaces could provide places for residents and visitors to meet, spend money and experience something distinctive to the town.

Rochdale's industrial history should not simply be something remembered in photographs. The surviving canal corridor provides an opportunity to use that history as part of the borough's future.

Environmental, regenerative and job-creation opportunities will follow if Rochdale is ambitious enough to recognise the potential sitting alongside its historic waterways.

The opportunity is there. The question is whether Rochdale is prepared to take it.

Steven Parker Rochdale Canal Group Originally written 8 September 2024.

articles.title: Watching Wednesday's solar eclipse? The glasses you need to protect your eyes
articles.excerpt: Rochdale is preparing for Wednesday's major partial solar eclipse - but ordinary sunglasses are not safe. Here's what to look for in eclipse glasses and how to watch safely.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale is preparing for one of the most spectacular astronomical events visible from Britain in years, with a major partial solar eclipse due to darken the skies on Wednesday 12 August.

But anyone planning to look up needs to get one thing sorted before Wednesday evening: ordinary sunglasses are not safe for watching a solar eclipse.

Specialist solar-eclipse glasses are designed to reduce the Sun's radiation to a level suitable for direct viewing. The important marking to look for is ISO 12312-2, the international safety standard covering filters used for direct observation of the Sun.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich advises eclipse watchers to use purpose-made solar viewing protection. Eclipse glasses should be inspected before use and should not be used if the filter is scratched, torn, punctured or otherwise damaged.

WHAT SHOULD YOU BUY?

Rochdale Daily has found Astral Solar Eclipse Paper Glasses from Absolute Eclipse, designed specifically for direct solar viewing. The retailer states that the glasses comply with EN ISO 12312-2:2015 and use specialist solar-filter material.

Single pairs are advertised at approximately £4.30 based on the retailer's euro price and current exchange rates, although the exact sterling amount charged may vary with the exchange rate and payment provider. Multipacks are also available for families and groups.

BUY ASTRAL SOLAR ECLIPSE GLASSES: https://absoluteeclipse.eu/products/astral-solar-eclipse-paper-glasses?sca_ref=12037834.ocoapNfFOz&sca_source=Rochdaledaily

Rochdale Daily may receive a commission if readers purchase through the link above. This does not increase the price paid by the customer.

WHY AREN'T SUNGLASSES ENOUGH?

Even extremely dark conventional sunglasses are designed for everyday daylight, not staring directly at the Sun. During an eclipse, the reduction in visible daylight can also create a false sense that looking towards the Sun has become safer. It has not.

Looking directly at the Sun without appropriate protection can damage the retina at the back of the eye. Crucially, retinal injury may occur without immediate pain, meaning somebody may not realise damage has occurred while they are watching.

Purpose-made eclipse glasses meeting the appropriate solar-viewing standard or an indirect viewing method such as a pinhole projector should therefore be used.

CHECK YOUR GLASSES BEFORE PUTTING THEM ON

Before Wednesday's eclipse, check the solar-filter material carefully. If you find scratches, holes, tears, punctures or other damage, do not use that pair.

Put your eclipse glasses on before looking towards the Sun and turn away from the Sun before removing them. Children should be supervised to make sure the glasses remain correctly positioned while they are looking upwards.

There is another important distinction: eclipse glasses are intended for unaided viewing with your eyes. They should not be used to look through binoculars, telescopes or camera lenses. Optical equipment concentrates sunlight and requires correctly fitted specialist solar filters designed for that equipment.

WHAT IF YOU CAN'T GET GLASSES IN TIME?

You can still experience the eclipse without looking directly at the Sun. A simple pinhole projector allows sunlight to pass through a small opening and project an image of the partially eclipsed Sun onto another surface.

Whatever method you choose, do not improvise with ordinary sunglasses, tinted glass or homemade eye filters.

WHEN CAN ROCHDALE SEE IT?

The eclipse takes place on Wednesday 12 August, beginning in the early evening and reaching maximum coverage shortly after 7pm in the Greater Manchester area. Around nine-tenths of the Sun is expected to be obscured at maximum, weather permitting.

It should create an extraordinary sight across Rochdale - but the most important preparation is making sure everyone watching has suitable eye protection before looking towards the Sun.

articles.title: Rare partial solar eclipse will be visible over Rochdale on Wednesday
articles.excerpt: A major partial solar eclipse will be visible across the UK on Wednesday 12 August, with around nine-tenths of the Sun expected to be obscured from the Rochdale area if skies remain clear.
articles.content_html:
People across Rochdale will have the chance to see one of the most striking astronomical events visible from the UK in years when a partial solar eclipse takes place on Wednesday 12 August.

The Met Office says the extent of the Sun's coverage and the precise timing of maximum obscuration will vary across the country, while local cloud and weather conditions will determine how much people are actually able to see.

Across the UK the eclipse will be substantial. Northeast Scotland is expected to see around 88 per cent of the Sun covered shortly before 7pm, while the far southwest of England will see around 96 per cent coverage shortly after 7.15pm.

For Greater Manchester and Rochdale, the eclipse is expected to begin at around 6.13pm, reach maximum obscuration at approximately 7.10pm and finish shortly after 8pm. Around 90 per cent of the Sun is expected to be covered at maximum, although the exact figure varies slightly by location.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich says the 12 August eclipse will be the largest partial solar eclipse visible from the UK and Ireland since 1999.

WEATHER COULD MAKE OR BREAK THE VIEW

Even a major eclipse can disappear behind typical British cloud, so anyone hoping to watch it should check the latest local forecast on the day. Thin or broken cloud may still allow glimpses, while thicker cloud could block the event completely.

HOW TO WATCH SAFELY

The Met Office stresses that people must never look directly at the Sun. Ordinary sunglasses are not safe for viewing an eclipse.

Certified eclipse glasses designed specifically for direct solar viewing can be used if they are undamaged and meet the appropriate safety standard. Another safe option is a pinhole projector, which allows the Sun's image to be projected onto a surface without looking directly at it.

Cameras, binoculars and telescopes should never be pointed at the Sun unless they are fitted with specialist solar filters designed for the equipment. Looking through an optical device without suitable protection can cause severe and permanent eye injury.

For residents lucky enough to get clear skies, Wednesday evening should provide a rare opportunity to see daylight noticeably dim as the Moon passes across most of the Sun's disc.

The Met Office has highlighted that the extent of the Sun's coverage and the exact time of maximum obscuration will vary across the country, while local cloud cover could make the difference between a clear view and missing the event entirely.

For Rochdale and the wider Greater Manchester area, timings are expected to be similar to Manchester and Liverpool. The Royal Observatory Greenwich says the eclipse should begin at around 6.13pm, reach maximum coverage at around 7.10pm and end shortly after 8pm.

Around 90 per cent of the Sun is expected to be obscured from much of the UK, with coverage increasing further towards the south-west. The Met Office says northeast Scotland will see around 88 per cent coverage shortly before 7pm, while parts of far south-west England could see around 96 per cent just after 7.15pm.

The eclipse will take place with the Sun relatively low in the western sky, so anyone hoping to watch from Rochdale may get the best view from an open location with a clear western horizon.

Weather will be crucial. The Met Office is advising people to check the local forecast in advance because cloud could obscure some or all of the eclipse.

There is also an important safety warning. People should never look directly at the Sun during an eclipse. Ordinary sunglasses are not enough. Safe options include certified eclipse glasses designed for solar viewing or indirect methods such as a pinhole projector.

The Royal Observatory Greenwich says the 12 August event will be the largest partial eclipse visible from the UK and Ireland since 1999, when a total eclipse was visible from parts of Cornwall and Devon.

Those unable to get a clear view locally will also have the option of watching live online, with the Royal Observatory planning a free livestream of the event.

Rochdale Daily will publish an updated local forecast closer to Wednesday so residents can see whether conditions are likely to cooperate.

articles.title: Every secondary school in Rochdale ranked: GCSEs, behaviour, attendance, Ofsted and what happens after Year 11
articles.excerpt: A parent's guide to the borough's 13 mainstream secondary schools - looking beyond GCSE league tables to behaviour, destinations, SEND provision, pastoral support and enrichment.
articles.content_html:
Choosing a secondary school is one of the biggest decisions a parent makes.

But deciding which school is "best" is considerably more complicated than looking at a GCSE league table.

A school could achieve excellent examination results while struggling with attendance. Another might have lower attainment but exceptional pastoral support, SEND provision and behaviour. A third might excel at getting pupils into college, apprenticeships or employment.

So Rochdale Daily has taken a broader look.

We have examined the latest publicly available information for the 13 mainstream secondary schools listed by Rochdale Borough Council, considering: Attainment 8; grade 5+ in English and mathematics; EBacc participation and performance; post-16 destinations; attendance; suspensions and behaviour; Ofsted findings; pastoral support; SEND provision; personal development; and extra-curricular opportunities.

The result is intended as a parent's guide rather than an official government league table.

There is also an important gap in the national data.

Why there is no Progress 8 score this year

Progress 8 would ordinarily be one of the most useful measures because it asks how much progress pupils make between primary school and GCSEs rather than simply how high their final grades are.

But the Department for Education cannot calculate Progress 8 for either 2024/25 or 2025/26 because pupils in those cohorts did not have the necessary Key Stage 2 assessment baseline following Covid disruption.

That means this year's Attainment 8 figures measure where pupils finished — not how far the school moved them from their starting point. That distinction matters.

Nationally, state-school pupils achieved an average Attainment 8 score of 46, while 45.4% achieved grade 5 or better in both English and mathematics. Across Rochdale, those figures were 40.6 and 35% respectively.

1. Hollingworth Academy, Milnrow — best academic performer

Hollingworth sits at the top primarily because its latest examination performance is significantly ahead of the Rochdale average. Its 2025 figures show an Attainment 8 score of 51.1, with 59.8% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths and an EBacc average point score of 4.48.

That means Hollingworth's Attainment 8 score was more than 10 points above the Rochdale average of 40.6 and also above the national state-school average of 46. The school's own 2025 figures similarly report an Attainment 8 score of around 51 and 60% achieving strong passes in English and maths.

There is, however, an interesting weakness. Only 22.2% entered the EBacc, compared with 40.5% nationally. And its published destination data for the 2023 leavers shows 84% of disadvantaged pupils continuing in education, apprenticeship or employment, compared with 94% of non-disadvantaged pupils nationally.

So although Hollingworth comfortably leads academically, parents should not interpret first place as meaning it dominates every measure.

Strengths: GCSE attainment, English and mathematics, broad academic performance. Watch: EBacc entry and destination gap among disadvantaged pupils.

2. Oulder Hill Leadership Academy — strongest all-round improvement story

Oulder Hill deserves to be near the top because the picture today is substantially different from that of its predecessor school. Its latest 2025 data gives an Attainment 8 score of 44.4, with 46.2% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths — the latter above both the Rochdale average and around the national level.

The more important finding comes from Ofsted. Following its January 2025 inspection, inspectors judged the quality of education, behaviour and attitudes, personal development, and leadership and management all Good.

That's particularly significant because the predecessor Oulder Hill Community School had previously been judged Inadequate before conversion to the Star Academies trust. Ofsted also confirmed that the school meets requirements for giving pupils access to information about technical education and apprenticeships.

Oulder Hill therefore performs particularly well in this ranking because it combines respectable attainment with strong independent inspection findings on behaviour, personal development and leadership.

Strengths: Behaviour, personal development, improving academic results, careers provision. Watch: Academic attainment remains below the national Attainment 8 average.

3. Wardle Academy — strong pastoral and academic balance

Wardle's 2025 Attainment 8 score was 44.1, above Rochdale's 40.6 average although still just below England's 46. Around 39.1% achieved grade 5+ in English and mathematics, also above the Rochdale borough figure of 35%.

But Wardle gets additional credit because the evidence isn't purely academic. The school was rated Good at its most recent Ofsted inspection, with inspectors reporting that pupils feel safe and happy and highlighting the strong relationships between pupils and staff and the school's pastoral approach.

Wardle also has specialist resourced SEND provision, something that may matter far more than league-table position for families of children with additional needs.

Strengths: Good Ofsted judgement, pastoral support, SEND provision, above-borough academic attainment. Watch: Results are solid rather than exceptional nationally.

4. St Cuthbert's RC High School — outstanding post-school destination performance

St Cuthbert's latest published results show an Attainment 8 score of 39.66, with 27.31% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 19% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.36. Those academic results place the school below Rochdale's overall averages.

But one number changes the picture considerably. The school reports 93.69% of pupils staying in education or entering employment after Key Stage 4.

That is precisely why simply ranking schools by GCSEs can mislead parents. St Cuthbert's examination figures are not among the borough's strongest, yet almost 94% of its leavers are progressing onwards.

Strengths: Post-16 destinations. Watch: GCSE attainment and strong passes in English and mathematics.

5. Cardinal Langley RC High School, Middleton — excellent destinations despite weaker 2025 attainment

Cardinal Langley's latest published government figures show an Attainment 8 score of 40.9, with 31.8% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 29.5% EBacc entry, an EBacc average point score of 3.46 — and 94% of leavers progressing to education, employment or an apprenticeship.

That 94% destination figure is excellent. The academic picture is more mixed: Attainment 8 is around the Rochdale average while English and mathematics strong passes remain below both borough and national levels.

Its position therefore reflects a strong record of getting pupils into their next destination even where the latest GCSE headline statistics are less remarkable.

Strengths: Destinations, post-16 progression. Watch: English and mathematics attainment.

6. Holy Family RC & CE College, Heywood — strong ethos and pastoral environment

Holy Family is particularly difficult to judge solely through a numerical league table because some of the most compelling evidence concerns school culture. Its most recent established Ofsted judgement is Good, while its denominational inspection rated the college Outstanding.

The school describes itself as an oversubscribed joint Roman Catholic and Church of England college and places a particularly strong emphasis on pastoral care, personal development and Christian ethos. For parents prioritising school environment alongside results, Holy Family deserves to sit toward the upper half of the table.

Strengths: Pastoral environment, ethos, inspection record. Watch: Parents should compare the latest individual GCSE subject outcomes when making an academic comparison with the schools above.

7. Dixons Middleton Academy — middle of the pack academically, Good Ofsted

Dixons Middleton recorded an Attainment 8 score of 40.3, with 33.6% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 42.9% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.57.

The EBacc entry rate is notable because it exceeds the Rochdale borough average and is around the national level. The school is rated Good by Ofsted, and its latest published destinations data indicates approximately 90% continuing into education, employment or apprenticeships.

The wider picture isn't perfect. Historical Parent View data collected around the 2024 inspection showed considerable disagreement among parents over behaviour and communication, although Parent View samples are voluntary and should never be treated like a representative opinion poll.

Strengths: EBacc participation, Good Ofsted judgement. Watch: Overall attainment and English/maths strong passes.

8. Falinge Park High School — around borough average with notable challenges

Government data for the predecessor establishment recorded an Attainment 8 score of 40.5, with 36.1% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 24.8% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.37. Those figures are remarkably close to Rochdale's overall results.

But Falinge serves a particularly challenging intake. Among disadvantaged pupils, Attainment 8 was 36.6, while 30.3% achieved strong passes in English and mathematics.

Interestingly, pupils with English as an additional language actually outperformed the school's overall cohort on several measures: EAL pupils recorded an Attainment 8 score of 42.6 compared with 40.5 overall. That is an important achievement which a simplistic league table would completely miss.

The school has since converted to academy status, meaning some current government tables show no comparable data under the new establishment record.

Strengths: Outcomes for EAL pupils. Watch: Overall attainment and disadvantaged-pupil gap.

9. Newhouse Academy, Heywood — behaviour stronger than academic outcomes

Newhouse recorded an Attainment 8 score of 38.9, with 29.7% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 30.8% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.26. That places academic performance below both Rochdale and national averages.

Its Ofsted picture is more encouraging. Although its 2023 inspection resulted in Requires Improvement overall, inspectors judged behaviour and attitudes, personal development, and leadership and management all Good. The school also underwent a monitoring visit in June 2025.

Newhouse has a substantial pastoral and attendance operation, including dedicated pastoral managers and an education welfare officer, with pupils' attendance monitored weekly. This is therefore another school where the headline GCSE statistics don't tell the full story.

Strengths: Behaviour, personal development, pastoral and attendance infrastructure. Watch: Academic attainment remains below borough averages.

10. Matthew Moss High School — academic outcomes currently below borough average

Matthew Moss recorded an Attainment 8 score of 39.3, with 34.3% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 26% EBacc entry and an EBacc average point score of 3.37. These figures put the school slightly below Rochdale's overall attainment measures.

Its disadvantaged cohort recorded an Attainment 8 score of 34.7, with 27.5% obtaining grade 5+ in English and mathematics.

The gender difference is also substantial: girls achieved an Attainment 8 score of 42.3, compared with 36 for boys. That is potentially one of the more interesting findings in the borough and deserves further investigation.

Strengths: Some stronger performance among girls and EAL pupils. Watch: Overall attainment and attainment among disadvantaged pupils and boys.

11. Kingsway Park High School — results weak, enrichment exceptionally interesting

On GCSE figures alone, Kingsway Park would sit near the bottom. Latest government figures show an Attainment 8 score of 35.3, with around 18% achieving grade 5+ in English and maths, 18.7% EBacc entry, an EBacc average point score of 2.87 — and 91% progressing to a recognised destination.

But Kingsway Park is perhaps the clearest demonstration of why this ranking goes beyond GCSE results. The school has developed an unusually extensive enrichment programme aimed particularly at children living in poverty, with reported activities including Brazilian jiu-jitsu, football, boxing, lacrosse, windsurfing, theatre, free music tuition and instruments for pupils. The school has also operated practical support including a food bank and assistance for families experiencing hardship.

Headteacher Simon Ward has spoken openly about tackling behaviour problems and attempting to provide opportunities pupils might otherwise never experience.

That does not erase weak examination performance. But it means describing Kingsway Park simply as one of Rochdale's "worst schools" would be unfair and potentially meaningless to a parent whose priority is enrichment, belonging or pastoral support.

Strengths: Enrichment, pastoral intervention, opportunities for disadvantaged children. Watch: GCSE attainment remains substantially below borough and national levels.

12. St Anne's CE Academy, Middleton — strong personal-development offer but academic comparison remains difficult

St Anne's was judged Good across all criteria by Ofsted in 2024. The academy describes a broad programme of extra-curricular activities alongside updated science and IT facilities and a nurturing Christian environment open to pupils of all faiths and backgrounds. This gives it a stronger qualitative picture than a purely exam-based comparison might suggest.

Strengths: Ofsted, enrichment, personal development and ethos. Watch: Comparable current GCSE data should be considered alongside the qualitative strengths before parents make a decision.

Edgar Wood Academy — not fairly rankable yet

Edgar Wood deserves a separate category. It is a relatively new school and the 2025 government performance tables show no Key Stage 4 cohort available for meaningful comparison. Trying to put it 13th simply because GCSE data doesn't exist would therefore be ridiculous.

The important evidence instead comes from Ofsted. The academy was inspected again in June 2026, following an earlier monitoring visit in May 2025. Because it is still developing and only recently reached the point at which older pupils move through the school, Rochdale Daily considers it unranked rather than last. That distinction matters.

What the league table tells us

There isn't actually one "best school" for every child.

If GCSE results are your priority, Hollingworth Academy is currently the clear standout: its 51.1 Attainment 8 score and approximately 60% strong-pass rate in English and mathematics are comfortably ahead of the borough averages.

If behaviour and personal development matter, Oulder Hill, Wardle, Newhouse and St Anne's have particularly useful independent inspection evidence.

If SEND provision is critical, parents should look beyond league tables altogether. Wardle, for example, has dedicated resourced provision. SEND arrangements differ significantly between schools and between individual children's needs.

If destinations matter, St Cuthbert's and Cardinal Langley both report approximately 94% progressing into education, employment or other recognised destinations.

If extracurricular opportunity matters, Kingsway Park's enrichment offer stands out despite comparatively weak academic figures.

And what about attendance and suspensions?

These deserve particular attention. Across Rochdale as a whole, secondary-school suspension levels have been sufficiently high to warrant concern, but using borough-wide numbers to label an individual school would be unfair.

Suspensions can also be counter-intuitive. A school recording more suspensions may genuinely have worse behaviour. But it may instead have a stricter behaviour policy and suspend pupils for conduct another school manages internally. Likewise, low suspensions don't automatically prove excellent behaviour.

That is why Rochdale Daily considers suspension data alongside Ofsted's behaviour and attitudes judgement, attendance, persistent absence and other evidence rather than awarding points simply for having fewer suspensions.

Attendance has similar complications. Schools serving communities experiencing severe deprivation, unstable housing, chronic illness or high levels of additional need can face greater attendance problems that are not entirely within the school's control. It remains an important measure — but it requires context.

Rochdale remains behind nationally on attainment

The wider borough picture shouldn't be ignored. Across Rochdale, the averages are: Attainment 8, 40.6; grade 5+ English and maths, 35%; EBacc entry, 30.2%; EBacc average point score, 3.47. National state-school figures are: Attainment 8, 46; grade 5+ English and maths, 45.4%; EBacc entry, 40.5%; EBacc average point score, 4.09.

So although individual schools are doing exceptionally well, Rochdale as a borough continues to have a substantial secondary-attainment gap with England overall. That is arguably the biggest education story of all.

Rochdale Daily's overall guide

1. Hollingworth Academy — strongest academics. 2. Oulder Hill Leadership Academy — strongest recent all-round inspection picture. 3. Wardle Academy — strong academic/pastoral balance. 4. St Cuthbert's RC High School — excellent destinations. 5. Cardinal Langley RC High School — strong destinations. 6. Holy Family RC & CE College — strong ethos and pastoral environment. 7. Dixons Middleton Academy — solid all-round performer. 8. Falinge Park High School — around borough average, noteworthy EAL outcomes. 9. Newhouse Academy — improving with good behaviour and personal development findings. 10. Matthew Moss High School — below-average current attainment. 11. Kingsway Park High School — weak attainment but exceptional enrichment story. 12. St Anne's CE Academy — Good inspection and broad enrichment; insufficient comparable attainment evidence for a higher position. Unranked: Edgar Wood Academy — too new for a fair full academic comparison.

A word to parents

A league table should be the beginning of choosing a school, not the end.

A child with SEND may thrive somewhere completely different from the highest-scoring GCSE school. A child struggling emotionally may benefit more from exceptional pastoral support. An academically driven pupil may be better suited to a school with particularly strong examination outcomes and curriculum breadth. A child who needs confidence may flourish because of sport, music, drama or enrichment.

Parents should therefore look at results, behaviour, attendance, pastoral care, SEND provision, destinations, enrichment — and how their own child feels inside the school. That gives a much more meaningful picture than a GCSE percentage alone.

Sources and methodology: Rochdale Daily's analysis uses the Department for Education's 2025 school performance tables, latest available Ofsted inspections and monitoring visits, Rochdale Borough Council's official secondary-school list, schools' statutory published information and publicly available destination, SEND, pastoral and enrichment information. Where directly comparable current information was unavailable, this is stated rather than estimated. Progress 8 has deliberately not been used for 2025 because the Department for Education says it cannot be calculated for the current cohorts due to the absence of Key Stage 2 baseline assessments following Covid disruption.

articles.title: One urgent care centre for 220,000 people: does Rochdale not deserve a real hospital?
articles.excerpt: Fifteen years after losing its A&E and maternity unit, Rochdale relies on a minor-injuries urgent care centre while its emergencies travel to Bury, Oldham and Manchester. Research shows distance to emergency care carries a measurable mortality risk.
articles.content_html:
A borough of 220,000 people. One urgent care facility. No A&E, no maternity unit, no children's ward. Is that really adequate for Rochdale?

Rochdale Infirmary is open, and its staff do valuable work. The Whitehall Street site runs a 24/7 Urgent Care Centre, a short-stay Clinical Assessment Unit, day surgery, a rheumatology centre, x-ray, blood testing, antenatal clinics, an early pregnancy unit, outpatient clinics and an eye unit. But the NHS's own description is blunt: there is no A&E at Rochdale Infirmary. The Urgent Care Centre treats minor injury and illness. It is the fourth smallest hospital in the Northern Care Alliance.

That is what remains of a hospital that, within living memory, was a proper district general. The A&E department closed in 2011. The maternity unit went the same way, along with the children's ward and, over the past two decades, ward after ward of acute provision - each removal justified at the time as centralisation, each leaving Rochdale residents travelling further for care.

Today, a Rochdale resident with a genuine emergency is sent to Fairfield in Bury, the Royal Oldham, or North Manchester General. On a good day, that is a manageable journey. In an ambulance queue, at rush hour, or for a family without a car relying on two buses, it is anything but. Every expectant mother in the borough gives birth outside it.

Does distance cost lives? The honest answer is that nobody publishes a Rochdale-specific figure, and we will not invent one. No official body calculates the percentage of local deaths that could have been avoided if a full hospital were closer, and any number we quoted would be guesswork. What does exist is peer-reviewed national research. A study of over 10,000 life-threatening emergency cases, published in the Emergency Medicine Journal by University of Sheffield researchers, found that the risk of death rose as the journey to hospital lengthened - from 5.8% for patients living under 10km away to 8.8% for those more than 20km away, with each additional 10km associated with around a one percentage point increase in mortality. Distance to emergency care is not a neutral fact. It is a clinical risk factor.

That research does not prove any individual Rochdale death was avoidable. It does mean the burden of proof should sit with those who decided that a borough of 220,000 people - larger than many towns and cities with a full district general hospital - can safely be served by a minor injuries facility.

The underuse of the Infirmary compounds the frustration. The site exists. The buildings exist. A workforce exists. Yet its role has been steadily narrowed rather than rebuilt, even as the borough's population has grown and the hospitals absorbing Rochdale's emergencies report some of the longest waits in the country. If capacity across north-east Greater Manchester is the problem - and A&E waiting figures suggest it is - then an under-used hospital estate in the middle of a 220,000-person borough looks less like a rational configuration and more like an inherited decision nobody has had the courage to revisit.

We asked whether the borough's elected representatives have taken a public position on restoring acute services to the Infirmary. We could find no current on-record statements from the borough's MPs or councillors specifically committing to that goal, and rather than paraphrase old campaign material we have chosen to put the question directly: does Rochdale's political leadership believe the current provision is adequate for this borough - and if not, what are they doing about it? We will publish their answers in full.

Fifteen years on from losing its A&E, the question for Rochdale is no longer how the services went, but why a borough this size should not expect them back. A fully equipped hospital - with an emergency department, a maternity unit and the wards this town has lost - is not nostalgia. For 220,000 people, it is the level of provision most comparable boroughs would consider a baseline.

If you are seriously ill or injured, always call 999 or attend your nearest A&E. The Urgent Care Centre at Rochdale Infirmary remains open 24/7 for minor injuries and illness, and NHS 111 can advise on the right service.

articles.title: End of the Wheatsheaf: demolition plans would replace Rochdale's empty shopping centre with 443 homes
articles.excerpt: Shut since 2020, the 1990-built centre could be flattened for apartments, townhouses and a new public square linking Yorkshire Street to Riverside. And no - we could find no record of a collapsed Primark deal.
articles.content_html:
The Wheatsheaf Shopping Centre - shut since the pandemic and increasingly an emblem of the high street Rochdale used to have - could finally be coming down.

The centre's Dubai-based owner, DHA Corporates, is working with Muse Architects on proposals to demolish the 168,000 sq ft complex and replace it with around 443 new homes: three apartment buildings and a row of townhouses, on current working figures roughly 134 one-bed apartments, 201 two-beds, 86 three-beds and 22 townhouses. The scheme would also include ten ground-floor commercial units, a community hub building and a significant new area of public space, designed to reconnect Yorkshire Street with the amenities at Rochdale Riverside to the south. An outline planning application is expected before the end of the year.

It would draw a line under three decades of mixed fortunes. The Wheatsheaf opened in 1990, originally linked to the former bus station and the "black box" council offices that stood where Rochdale Riverside now sits. In its heyday it was a bustling complex of five floors, home to some 15 big-name stores and independent retailers, with names like Wilko, Argos, New Look and Peacocks trading there over the years - plus the town's library on its upper floors before the move to Number One Riverside.

The decline was long and visible. Wilko pulled out in 2018 when its lease expired. The centre closed with the rest of the country in the March 2020 lockdown, briefly reopened, closed again that November - and then its then owner, MCR Property Group, announced it would not reopen at all, blaming the shift to online shopping and a retail environment that had become unsustainable. It has stood vacant ever since. DHA Corporates bought the building in 2022 for around £3m, and last year won permission to convert part of it into a wedding and banqueting venue - a scheme that is no longer going ahead in favour of the residential plan.

Readers have asked about a reported deal with Primark said to have collapsed when the retailer was refused permission to trade until 8pm. Rochdale Daily has been unable to find any record of such a deal or any published account of Primark negotiating for space at the Wheatsheaf, and there is no Primark store in Rochdale town centre. We are happy to hear from anyone with documented information, but we cannot report the claim as fact.

The bigger question is what the Wheatsheaf's story says about the town centre around it. The opening of Rochdale Riverside in 2020 concentrated the big names - M&S, Next, H&M, a cinema - on one modern site, and much of the older retail circuit has never recovered. Footfall on Yorkshire Street is a fraction of what it once was, and the units that remain trading lean heavily towards charity shops, discount stores and vape shops rather than the varied high street older residents remember. In that context, hundreds of new town centre homes may do more for Rochdale's shops than another retail scheme ever could: people who live in the centre spend in the centre.

Nothing is decided yet. The proposals must still go through the planning process, and residents will have the chance to comment when the outline application is submitted. But after six years of a dead shopping centre at the heart of the town, the direction of travel is now clear: the Wheatsheaf's future is homes, not shops.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC recruiting for five roles across first team, academy and women's side ahead of League Two return
articles.excerpt: Promotion back to the Football League means growth off the pitch too: Dale are hiring a kit assistant, performance analysts, an academy lead coach and a women's first team physio.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC has announced five vacancies across the club as it gears up for life back in the Football League.

The roles span the men's first team, the academy and the women's first team: a kit assistant, two performance analysts, a youth development phase lead coach and a women's first team physiotherapist or sports therapist.

The recruitment drive is a direct consequence of the club's growth. Jim McNulty's side won promotion back to Sky Bet League Two at Wembley in May, ending three seasons in the National League, and a return to the EFL brings bigger demands across every department - from matchday operations to sports science and the academy.

The kit assistant role, focused on the men's first team, is aimed at someone passionate about providing excellent service across the club's teams, with applications closing at 5pm on Friday 14 August. The club is also seeking a men's first team performance analysis work placement student for the 2026/27 season - a role suited to a student taking a sandwich year in an undergraduate degree, though masters students and recent graduates seeking industry experience will be considered.

On the academy side, Rochdale is recruiting a youth development phase lead coach. Applicants must hold a UEFA A Licence and relevant youth coaching qualifications, with previous experience in a professional academy environment an advantage. The club has said academy positions are subject to a Category 3 licence under the Elite Player Performance Plan being awarded this summer - a significant step for an academy that has long punched above its weight in producing first-team players.

The women's first team is recruiting a physiotherapist or sports therapist on a part-time, sessional basis, covering all women's first team fixtures, at least one training session a week, and injury rehabilitation and gym-based work.

The vacancies come with the 2026/27 campaign only just under way. Dale opened their season with a Carabao Cup preliminary round trip to Tranmere Rovers, and the League Two campaign is in its opening days - far too early for the table to tell us anything meaningful about how the newly promoted side will fare. The summer has brought new faces to Sandy Lane, including French midfielder Gomez-Mancini, midfielder Humbles, and Jason Taylor joining the coaching staff.

Full job adverts, including details of how to apply, are available on the club's website at rochdaleafc.co.uk, with any further academy vacancies listed on the EFL's iRecruit platform.

articles.title: Fraudsters who fought over the pensioners they were fleecing jailed - Rochdale woman among victims of £97,000 scam
articles.excerpt: Eight people have been sentenced over a roofing scam that took £97,000 from five elderly victims in three months - including £7,800 from a 77-year-old Rochdale woman. Two victims died before seeing justice.
articles.content_html:
A group of fraudsters who squabbled over the vulnerable pensioners they were ripping off have been jailed - including for a scam that stripped £7,800 from a 77-year-old Rochdale woman.

Eight people have now been sentenced over a ruthless building scam that took around £97,000 from five elderly victims across England in the space of just three months. They pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud and related money laundering offences.

The fraudsters pressured pensioners into handing over cash, making bank transfers and signing large cheques for roof repairs that were never carried out.

The 77-year-old woman from Rochdale was pressured into handing over cash, making transfers and signing cheques totalling £7,800, forced to dip into savings to pay for work that was never done.

Some of the most disturbing details emerged when police examined messages recovered from the offenders' phones. Two rival groups of scammers had independently targeted the same vulnerable man in Ellesmere Port. They regularly took him to local cash machines and made him withdraw money, and also used his bank card to buy themselves food and groceries. As his money ran out, the two rival factions clashed over who had the right to keep defrauding him.

The offending only came to light when the man's regular direct debits started to bounce because his account had been drained, and he turned to a friend for help.

Other victims included an elderly man in Ellesmere Port persuaded to write cheques worth £34,500 for roof work that was never completed, an elderly woman in Coventry whose signed blank cheques were written out for £13,000, and an elderly woman in Corby who had unnecessary roof repairs carried out to a poor standard.

The stolen money was laundered through the bank accounts of several accomplices before being spent on expensive meals and luxury Rolex watches.

Tragically, two of the elderly victims died before the gang finally appeared in court and never saw justice served.

Detective Constable Rob Mackay, of Ellesmere Port CID, who led the investigation, described it as a lengthy and complex inquiry.

The case is a reminder of how doorstep criminals operate: unsolicited callers claiming urgent roof or building problems, pressure to pay immediately in cash or by cheque, and escorted trips to the bank. Trading standards advice is never to agree to work from a cold caller, to seek quotes from traders you approach yourself, and to talk to a trusted friend or family member before parting with money. Anyone who believes an elderly relative or neighbour is being targeted can contact police on 101, or Action Fraud.

articles.title: RBH warns tenants over cold-calling 'claims farmers' offering compensation for repairs
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Boroughwide Housing says customers are being cold-called by firms offering 'no win, no fee' solicitors for repair claims - a warning that lands against the backdrop of the Awaab Ishak tragedy and the reforms that followed.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Boroughwide Housing has warned tenants to be on their guard after a number of customers reported being cold-called by a firm asking about property repairs.

The landlord says the callers offered to provide a solicitor to work on tenants' behalf so they could claim compensation. Firms operating this way - sometimes called claims management companies or "claims farmers" - typically describe themselves as offering "no win, no fee" services.

"Be careful - if something sounds too good to be true, it probably is," RBH said, urging anyone with a concern about their home to talk to the landlord directly so it can be sorted. Repairs can be reported via the MyRBH portal at www.myrbh.org.uk, by calling Freephone 0800 027 7769, or by emailing rbh.repairs@rbh.org.uk. RBH says it aims to get things right first time, and tenants who feel it has fallen short can find details of how to complain at www.rbh.org.uk/feedback.

Why this matters in Rochdale

No warning about housing disrepair in this borough can be read in isolation from what happened to Awaab Ishak.

Awaab was two years old when he died in December 2020. In November 2022, a coroner concluded that his death was caused by prolonged exposure to mould in his family's RBH flat on the Freehold estate - mould his parents had repeatedly reported. The case caused national outrage, cost RBH its chief executive, and led directly to Awaab's Law, which sets legal time limits for social landlords in England to investigate and fix damp, mould and other hazards, with the first phase of those duties coming into force in October 2025.

That history cuts two ways. It explains why RBH is now at pains to encourage tenants to report repairs directly and to demonstrate that reports will be acted on - rebuilding confidence that was badly damaged. And it also explains why claims firms see RBH tenants as a market worth cold-calling: disrepair claims against social landlords have grown sharply across the country, and a landlord with RBH's recent history is an obvious target for firms seeking clients.

Tenants are entitled to seek independent legal advice about genuine disrepair, and nothing prevents them doing so. But consumer bodies have long warned that some claims firms take large cuts of any compensation, sign tenants up to agreements with exit fees, or pursue claims that leave tenants worse off than simply having the repair done. A tenant's first and simplest route remains reporting the problem to the landlord - and, if it is not fixed, escalating through the complaints process and then to the Housing Ombudsman, which is free.

The test for RBH is the one Awaab's case set: whether reports of damp, mould and disrepair are fixed properly and fast, first time. If they are, the cold-callers will find little to farm.

articles.title: Shoppers donate 368 kilos of food at Rochdale Foodbank's Morrisons Kingsway drive
articles.excerpt: Generous shoppers added extra items to their trolleys over two days at Morrisons Kingsway, donating 368kg of food. How the foodbank works, how to get help - and how to give it.
articles.content_html:
Shoppers at Morrisons Kingsway have donated a remarkable 368 kilos of food to Rochdale Foodbank after a two-day food drive at the store last Thursday and Friday.

The foodbank thanked all the generous shoppers who added extra items to their shopping, saying donations came in all shapes and sizes and included many of its most needed items. The charity also paid special tribute to the volunteers who staffed the collection and made the event a success, adding that every single item received will make a big difference to its clients.

Rochdale Foodbank has been part of life in the town for more than a decade. Registered as a charity in its own right in 2017, it operates as part of the Trussell network of food banks and is run almost entirely by volunteers - around 70 of them - who sort, date-check and pack donated food into emergency parcels at its base off Newgate in the town centre.

How the foodbank works

The foodbank operates on a referral system. Care professionals - including GPs, health visitors, social workers, Citizens Advice staff, welfare officers, the police and probation services - identify people in crisis and issue them with a foodbank voucher. That voucher can then be exchanged at a foodbank session for an emergency parcel containing at least three days of nutritionally balanced food. Volunteers meet clients over a cup of tea and can signpost them to agencies able to help with the longer-term problem, from debt advice to benefits support.

Alongside its main sessions, the foodbank has expanded in recent years. A Saturday morning session runs at Branches Christian Fellowship in Smallbridge, where clients can collect parcels between 10am and 12pm, and the charity has also opened Rochdale Central Pantry in the Rochdale Exchange Shopping Centre - a membership pantry for people who have recently needed foodbank support and could use a little extra help each week.

If you need help, you can call the foodbank on 0300 102 1646 or visit rochdale.foodbank.org.uk, which lists the organisations able to issue vouchers.

How to donate

More than nine in ten items given out by Trussell network food banks are donated by the public, which is why collections like the Morrisons drive matter so much. There are permanent donation points in Rochdale's larger supermarkets, including Tesco, Asda and Morrisons, intended for food purchased in-store. Larger donations can be dropped off at the foodbank's warehouse via the Newgate service area - ring ahead on 0300 102 1646 for big deliveries - and the foodbank publishes a shopping list of the items it most urgently needs on its website. Money donations, which help cover running costs and fill gaps in donated stock, can also be made through the website.

As the foodbank itself puts it: even if it's just one tin every week, every tin helps.

articles.title: Reform UK councillors explain vote against 74-bed Sparth House care home
articles.excerpt: All three Reform UK members of Rochdale's Planning Committee voted against the revised 74-bed care home at Sparth House, saying concerns over scale, trees and parking had not been resolved.
articles.content_html:
All three Reform UK councillors serving on Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee voted against the proposed 74-bed care home development at Sparth House, Manchester Road, when the application returned to the Committee.

The application had previously been deferred after members raised concerns regarding the scale and massing of the proposed building, its impact on neighbouring residents, the loss of mature trees, parking provision and whether the development represented an appropriate use of the site.

In a statement setting out their reasons, the Reform UK group said that when the revised application returned to Committee, its councillors remained of the view that those concerns had not been adequately addressed. Whilst amendments had been made to the application, the group said it did not believe they sufficiently overcame the fundamental planning issues that had led to the original deferral.

"Let us be absolutely clear," the statement said. "Reform UK fully supports investment in high-quality care facilities. We recognise the growing need for dementia and nursing care across Rochdale Borough, particularly as our population ages. However, supporting better care does not mean supporting every planning application regardless of its merits."

The group said every development must be judged on whether it is appropriate for its location, whether it protects neighbouring residents, whether it provides suitable living conditions for future occupants and whether local infrastructure is capable of supporting it.

In this case, the Reform UK councillors concluded that the proposed four-storey building represented an overdevelopment of a constrained site, arguing that its overall scale, height and massing would create an overbearing presence, harm the character of the surrounding area and adversely affect neighbouring residential amenity.

The councillors also said they were concerned by the environmental impact of the proposal, including the loss of mature trees, together with what they considered to be limited meaningful outdoor space for a development accommodating 74 vulnerable residents.

Parking provision remained another significant concern for the group. With 13 parking spaces proposed for staff, visitors, healthcare professionals and servicing vehicles, the councillors considered there to be a real risk of additional parking pressure on surrounding residential streets.

Whilst not a material planning consideration and ultimately a matter governed by Building Regulations, the group said members also noted concerns raised during the planning process regarding the practical challenges of evacuating a four-storey building occupied by elderly and vulnerable residents, including people living with dementia, in the event of an emergency. Although these matters fall outside the planning system, the councillors said they nevertheless formed part of the wider public concerns expressed during the application process.

The statement also criticised the local MP, Elsie Blundell, who the group said had commented critically on the decision on social media rather than engaging with the planning concerns debated by the Committee. "Planning decisions should be based on planning merits, evidence and policy, not reduced to political point scoring," the group said. Ms Blundell has been invited to respond, and any reply will be added to this article.

The Reform UK councillors said their responsibility as Planning Committee members is not to approve applications simply because they provide a particular type of development, but to consider every application impartially against planning policy, the evidence before them and the impact on both existing and future residents.

"Had this application demonstrated an appropriate scale, adequate infrastructure, sufficient parking, suitable landscaping and a design compatible with its surroundings, Reform UK would have had no hesitation in supporting it," the statement concluded. "Good care homes deserve good planning. Residents deserve developments that are both needed and appropriate. We will continue to stand up for both."

Planning applications refused by the Committee can be appealed by the applicant to the Planning Inspectorate.
